title: Did Cleopatra Really Die From an Asp Bite? What the Ancient Writers Actually Said
description: After Octavian's men found Cleopatra's body, what can a basket of figs, faint marks on her arm and a snake in the triumph actually prove? This episode follows the last days as recorded in Plutarch's Life of Antony, and sets them against the other versions in Suetonius's Life of Augustus and Cassius Dio's Roman History. All three authors wrote after the event; none was a witness inside the sealed room. A snakebite is one possible account, but how she actually died has never been proven. The illustrations are cartoon depictions. Sources checked on 2026-10-20.

chapters.cl001: A countryman shows a basket of figs
chapters.cl006: Antony is hauled into the tomb
chapters.cl019: Guards ordered to keep the queen alive
chapters.cl045: The sealed letter goes out, the door shuts
chapters.cl068: Dio moves the queen to the palace
chapters.cl077: Octavian tries a cure; the triumph carries a snake

cl001.text: Outside a tomb in Alexandria, a peasant with a basket of figs walks up to Cleopatra's guards.

cl002.text: The guards want to see inside; he lifts the leaves, and it's full of figs.

cl003.text: Later, one story said an asp hid under those figs. Did the guards really miss it?

cl004.text: Soon a sealed letter reaches Octavian, and he sends men back at once.

cl005.text: His men are about to open the door. Can the snake image in his later triumph reveal what happened inside?

cl006.text: Before the letter, the tomb's door was shut. The wounded Antony was carried to it.

cl007.text: Cleopatra drops ropes, and she and two maids haul him up.

cl008.text: Plutarch writes that Antony died at her side. The war is over; what choices does she have left?

cl009.text: Plutarch says Octavian feared losing the treasure and wanted her alive.

cl010.text: Both biographers mention the triumph: alive, she could be paraded in the victory march.

cl011.text: She stays in the tomb, door shut. Octavian sends Proculeius to talk.

cl012.text: She talks to him through the door. Can Proculeius get her to open it herself?

cl013.text: No. She's still in the tomb, but he notices a high window.

cl014.text: It's the window she pulled Antony through. Now the Romans have their eyes on it too.

cl015.text: Another envoy keeps talking at the door. How does Proculeius get in?

cl016.text: The biography says he took two men up a ladder, straight to her.

cl017.text: Cleopatra grabs a dagger. Is she in time?

cl018.text: He takes the dagger and searches her clothes for poison.

cl019.text: Octavian then puts guards on her: treat her gently, but never let her kill herself.

cl020.text: Plutarch notes another attempt: she once tried not eating, letting her life slowly end. Would Octavian let her go on?

cl021.text: Plutarch says this comes from an account by her physician, Olympus.

cl022.text: Octavian suspects it, and uses her children's safety to make her eat again.

cl023.text: When the Roman commander visits in person, she rises from her bed to plead.

cl024.text: She says she feared Antony and tries to defend her choices. He rebuts her point by point.

cl025.text: She turns to begging, as if hoping to live longer. Does Octavian buy it?

cl026.text: She hands in a treasure list; her steward says items are missing.

cl027.text: She grabs him and angrily denies it. But why were items left off?

cl028.text: The biography says she meant to keep small gifts, so Octavian's family would speak for her.

cl029.text: Octavian lets her keep them and promises better treatment. Is he convinced?

cl030.text: Octavian decides she finally wants to live. The biography says he was wrong.

cl031.text: But Plutarch adds she had already enlisted a young man close to Octavian. Who?

cl032.text: His name is Dolabella, and as she asked, he quietly brings her news.

cl033.text: Octavian returns via Syria; she and her children will be sent off in three days.

cl034.text: If taken from Egypt, could she still lie beside Antony?

cl035.text: She asks Octavian to sacrifice at Antony's tomb. He agrees.

cl036.text: She's escorted to the tomb, her women beside her.

cl037.text: The biography has her say at the tomb she won't be taken far, and wants to lie with Antony.

cl038.text: She lays wreaths and kisses the tomb. Once back, what does she do before her meal?

cl039.text: Back home, she orders a bath.

cl040.text: After bathing, she eats a lavish meal. Who's at the door now?

cl041.text: It's that countryman, now coming with a small basket.

cl042.text: The guards stop him; he parts the leaves himself to show them the figs.

cl043.text: They even praise the big, fine figs, but take none.

cl044.text: So the basket goes in. The guards stay outside. What does the queen do next?

cl045.text: After dinner, she has a sealed letter sent to the Roman commander.

cl046.text: Then, Plutarch says, she sends everyone out except Iras and Charmion.

cl047.text: The door shuts. No survivor in the biography can tell us each step that followed.

cl048.text: Octavian reads her plea to be buried with Antony, and fears the worst.

cl049.text: He starts to go himself, then sends messengers; the guards suspect nothing. In time to save her?

cl050.text: The door opens. The queen is dead, in her royal robes.

cl051.text: Iras lies dying at the bed's foot; Charmion still props up the queen's diadem.

cl052.text: Plutarch adds that Charmion answered the men with one line, then fell.

cl053.text: The envoys were too late. Later, Octavian let her lie with Antony.

cl054.text: Octavian had her two women buried too.

cl055.text: The envoys saw only the outcome. How was the basket the guards let in explained?

cl056.text: That basket of figs from the start: some say an asp hid under its leaves.

cl057.text: This version says she moved the figs, saw the snake, and gave it her arm.

cl058.text: But the biography says "some say," not "the guards saw it."

cl059.text: Others say it was in a jar; she prodded it with a gold spindle.

cl060.text: The same author picks no winner. He writes: what really happened, no one knows.

cl061.text: Another path: she may have hidden poison in a hollow hairpin.

cl062.text: A hairpin as well as a snake. Can the marks on her body tell them apart?

cl063.text: Plutarch says: no obvious signs of poison, and no one saw the snake in the tomb.

cl064.text: Some claimed snake-like tracks in the sand by the sea; still just a rumor.

cl065.text: Others say her arm had two faint pricks; the biography doesn't treat it as settled.

cl066.text: Remember: once the door shut, no one saw each step. Marks found later can't fill that gap.

cl067.text: So it's snake or hairpin. Could Dio, writing later, tell which one is true?

cl068.text: Dio can't say how she died either, but he has her held somewhere else.

cl069.text: Plutarch leaves her in the tomb; Dio has her moved to the palace, with her usual attendants.

cl070.text: Dio adds she gave jewels as gifts and said she'd sail willingly, so the guards relaxed.

cl071.text: Dio says the body's arm showed only faint marks. Can that alone tell a fang from a pin?

cl072.text: He makes no call; he only says some hid a snake in a jar or flowers.

cl073.text: Others say the pin was poisoned. What act does this version even describe?

cl074.text: As Dio relates it, she cut her arm slightly, then let the pin touch the blood. Still hearsay.

cl075.text: Seeing her body, the Roman commander orders her revived. Can that prove the cause?

cl076.text: Dio doesn't use the rescue to give a cause. What tone does another author take here?

cl077.text: Suetonius says she was "believed" bitten by a snake, so Octavian had Psylli try to suck out the poison.

cl078.text: Octavian couldn't parade her alive, but something else marched in it.

cl079.text: Plutarch says Octavian's later triumph showed her image with a snake.

cl080.text: That image proves one thing: the snake version had become public victory art.

cl081.text: A carved snake isn't a witnessed bite. Which of the three writers can say they saw it?

cl082.text: That's why we ask "for sure?": none of the three surviving writers proves it.

cl083.text: Which picture did you believe most: the fig basket, or the snake in the triumph?

cl084.text: This channel sticks to ancient records. Subscribe to test the legends with us.
